article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 5-Question Quiz (Types I–VI)
article.meta_description: Take a simple Fitzpatrick skin type test, see what types I to VI mean, and learn why it isn't the same as skin tone or undertone for makeup and color.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 5-Question Quiz Plus Tie-Breaker, and What Your Result Means
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types (I to VI) based on how your skin tends to react to sun: whether it burns, tans, or shows little visible change. You can estimate a type with the five questions and tie-breaker below. The scale describes sun reaction only. It does not tell you your skin tone, your undertone, or which foundation and clothing colors suit you.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type scale based on how skin reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by a dermatologist as a way to describe how different skin responds to sunlight. Type I sits at one end (skin that burns very easily and barely tans) and Type VI at the other (very deeply pigmented skin that very rarely burns, if ever). Types II to V fall in between.

Why it is not the same as skin tone, undertone, or oily/dry skin type

People often mix up four different ideas:

  • Fitzpatrick type: how skin tends to react to sun.
  • Skin tone (depth): how light or deep your skin looks, from fair to very deep.
  • Undertone: the subtle warm, cool, neutral, or olive cast beneath the surface color. Olive is an undertone, not a depth.
  • Oily, dry, or combination skin: a separate, cosmetic way of describing how skin feels and looks through the day.

Who uses it, and why a self-test is only a rough guide

The scale comes from dermatology, where professionals use it as one reference point. A quiz you score yourself relies on memory and honesty, and most people's reactions don't fit neatly into six boxes. Treat your result as a rough label for curiosity, not as a professional opinion.

Before you start the Fitzpatrick skin type test

Think about your natural, unprotected skin, not a tan or a product

Answer for your skin as it is without a tan, self-tanner, or tinted product. For the color question, think of an area that rarely sees the sun, such as the inner upper arm.

Answer from experience, not a single holiday

One unusual trip, like a cloudy week or a day with heavy sunscreen, can skew your answer. Think about what usually happens across several years.

A pen-and-paper way to score your answers

Write down one number per question, then add them up. Questions 2, 3, and 5 are about sun reaction, which is what the scale is really about, so each is worth 0 to 4 points. Questions 1 and 4 (skin color, then eye and hair color) are only loose pigment clues, so each is worth just 0 to 2 points. The tie-breaker afterwards is not scored.

This is a simplified system made for this guide. It is not a clinical tool, and the score bands below have not been validated. They are only a rough way to organize your answers. Questionnaires used by professionals are longer and scored differently. If your skin is already very deep, read the notes under Questions 3 and 5 and the tie-breaker, because visible tanning is harder to notice on deeper skin.

The self-test: 5 questions and a tie-breaker

Question 1: What is your natural skin color in areas rarely exposed to sun? (0–2 points)

This question is about depth only. Don't factor in undertone here.

  • 0: Very pale, ivory, fair, or light
  • 1: Light-medium to medium (including light-to-medium brown)
  • 2: Medium-deep brown to very deep brown

Question 2: What happens after your first unprotected sun exposure of the season? (0–4 points)

  • 0: Always burns, often painfully, and may peel
  • 1: Usually burns
  • 2: Sometimes burns mildly
  • 3: Rarely burns
  • 4: Almost never burns

Question 3: Does your skin tan afterwards, and how deeply? (0–4 points)

Tanning is harder to see on deeper skin, so there is an option for that.

  • 0: No tan at all; skin goes red or freckles instead
  • 1: Tans slightly and slowly
  • 2: Tans gradually to a light brown
  • 3: Tans easily to a moderate brown
  • 4: Tans very easily and deepens quickly, or my skin is already very deep and I don't notice a visible change after sun, without redness or burning

Question 4: How do eye and natural hair color fit in? (a loose clue only, 0–2 points)

Eye and hair color are the weakest clue, because plenty of people don't match the typical pattern. Score it, but don't lean on it.

  • 0: Red or very light blonde hair, light blue or green eyes
  • 1: Blonde, light brown, or medium brown hair; blue, green, hazel, or light brown eyes
  • 2: Dark brown or black hair, dark brown eyes

Question 5: How does your skin react to repeated sun exposure over time? (0–4 points)

  • 0: Stays sensitive and burns again easily
  • 1: Burns less over time but still often
  • 2: Tans, with an occasional burn
  • 3: Tans and rarely burns
  • 4: Deepens in color or shows no visible change, and doesn't seem to burn

Tie-breaker: do your answers point to two neighboring types?

Add up your score from Questions 1 to 5 (0 to 16). If the total sits right on a band boundary, or your answers are scattered, read both neighboring types in the next section and go with the one that better matches your real-life sun history. If you chose the deepest option for Question 1 and "rarely" or "almost never" burns for Question 2, treat Types V and VI as equally possible rather than relying on the exact total.

Your result: Fitzpatrick types I to VI in plain language

Total score (rough, unvalidated bands)Estimated typeTypical sun reaction (general description)
0–2IBurns very easily, hardly tans
3–5IIBurns easily, tans minimally
6–8IIISometimes burns, tans gradually
9–11IVBurns rarely, tans easily
12–13VBurns very rarely, tans or deepens easily
14–16VIVery rarely or never burns, very deeply pigmented

Types I and II: skin that tends to burn easily

These types burn quickly and tan little or not at all. Type I is the most sun-reactive, and Type II is slightly less so.

Types III and IV: skin that burns sometimes and tans gradually

Type III tends to burn mildly at first and then tan. Type IV burns less often and tans more readily. These are common middle-of-the-scale results, and they cover a wide range of looks.

Types V and VI: skin that rarely burns and tans easily or is deeply pigmented

These types burn very rarely or not at all. That does not mean skin needs no sun protection (more on that below). On deep skin a tan may be subtle, so a lower score on the tanning question doesn't necessarily mean a lower type.

If you fall between types: why that is normal and what to do

Skin reactions vary with season, climate, and how much sun you've had recently, so landing between two types is common. You don't need to force a single answer. If a professional ever asks for your type, describe how your skin actually reacts and let them take it from there.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A quick comparison: what each one describes and what it is used for

Fitzpatrick typeSkin tone (depth)Undertone
DescribesSun reactionHow light or deep skin looksWarm, cool, neutral, or olive cast
How you find itQuestions about burning and tanningCompare your skin in natural lightVein, jewelry, and white-paper checks (limited reliability on their own)
Useful forA general reference point on sun reactionFoundation depth, color contrastFoundation, blush, lip, and clothing colors

To find the last two, see our guides on how to find your skin tone depth and undertone and five simple undertone tests.

Why two people with the same Fitzpatrick type can need different makeup shades

Two people can both land on Type IV, with one having a light-olive complexion and the other a medium-brown one. Their foundation shades, and the colors that flatter them, will be quite different. The type only describes sun reaction, so it can't pick a shade.

Where the scale falls short for describing the full range of skin tones

Six types cannot capture the huge variety of real skin tones and undertones, especially among deeper complexions, which get grouped into just a couple of categories. The scale also wasn't designed with makeup or wardrobe in mind. That is another reason not to use it for color decisions.

What to use for makeup and clothing colors instead

Find your depth and undertone

Check your skin in natural daylight near a window, without makeup. Note whether it reads fair, light, medium, tan, deep, or very deep, then work out whether the undertone is warm, cool, neutral, or olive using the guides linked above.

Consider your natural contrast

Contrast is the difference between your skin, hair, and eyes. High contrast (for example, deep hair against fair skin) often carries sharp pairings such as black with crisp white. Low contrast (soft hair and skin tones close together) often looks polished in tonal outfits, like oatmeal with camel or dusty blue with soft gray.

Cosmetic starting points for foundation, blush, lip, and wardrobe colors

  • Foundation: test three shades along the jawline in daylight and choose the one that disappears into your neck.
  • Warm or golden undertones: try peach or terracotta blush and coral or warm brick lips. For clothes, try olive, camel, rust, and cream.
  • Cool or pink undertones: try rose or berry blush and raspberry or mauve lips. For clothes, try navy, emerald, charcoal, and cool pinks.
  • Neutral undertones: you can often move between the warm and cool families. Try dusty rose, soft terracotta, and muted teal, then see which feels best in daylight.
  • Olive undertones: a greenish-golden cast often pairs well with earthy and jewel tones. Try warm berry or brick lips, and for clothes try forest green, plum, and warm taupe.

These are starting points, not rules. For more on matching makeup to your features, try our six-question makeup quiz.

Sun protection: what this test can't tell you

Sun protection matters for every skin tone and type

A low-burn result does not mean you can skip sun protection. Widely accepted general habits, such as sunscreen, shade, and protective clothing, apply to everyone. How much and what kind is a question for a health professional, not a quiz.

A quiz result is not a risk score or a professional opinion

This quiz is a style-and-curiosity exercise. A number from I to VI is only a rough label for sun reaction. It is not personal health guidance.

When to see a dermatologist or doctor

See a dermatologist or doctor about any skin concern, any change you notice in your skin, or questions about professional care. They can give advice specific to you, which no quiz or app can.

Where FitCheck AI fits in

What the live skin analysis does: a cosmetic skin overview with beauty suggestions

If you took this test hoping to choose makeup or colors, FitCheck AI's live skin analysis with your camera gives you an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. The app also has an AI makeup assistant, which offers personalized makeup suggestions and feedback based on your appearance, and a live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview a look such as lipstick on your own face with the live camera. Its color coordination guidance can help with which colors and combinations go together in your wardrobe. It is an Android app, free on Google Play, and iOS is coming soon.

The AI feedback is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern.

What it doesn't do: no Fitzpatrick type and no medical advice

The app cannot tell you your Fitzpatrick type or how your skin reacts to sun. Its feedback is a starting point and an AI opinion, not a professional opinion.

Photo tips: natural light, eye-level camera, no filters

For makeup and hair, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and avoid filters.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick skin type test accurate?
faqs.answer: A self-scored quiz is only a rough guide. It depends on how well you remember your own sun reactions, tanning is harder to notice on deeper skin, and many people sit between two types. Treat the result as a loose label, not a professional opinion.

faqs.question: Can the Fitzpatrick type tell me my foundation shade?
faqs.answer: No. The scale describes how skin reacts to sun, not how light or deep it looks or what undertone it has. For foundation, test shades along your jawline in natural light and work out your depth and undertone instead.

faqs.question: Can I be two Fitzpatrick types at once?
faqs.answer: Your answers can sit between two neighboring types, such as III and IV, or V and VI, and that's common. Skin reactions also shift with season and recent sun exposure. Describe how your skin actually behaves rather than forcing a single number.

faqs.question: Do darker skin tones still need sunscreen?
faqs.answer: Sun protection applies to every skin tone and type. General habits like sunscreen, shade, and protective clothing are widely recommended for everyone, including people who rarely burn. A dermatologist or doctor can give advice specific to you.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: FitCheck AI cannot. Its live skin analysis gives a cosmetic overview with beauty suggestions, not a Fitzpatrick type. The AI feedback is not medical advice, so see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern.

factual_issues: The tie-breaker contradicts the article's own scoring table. If someone picks the deepest option for Q1 and 'rarely burns' (3) for Q2, the total can easily land in the Type IV band (e.g. 2+3+2+2+2 = 11). The tie-breaker still tells them to treat Types V and VI as 'equally possible' and not to rely on the total. That skips Type IV, which is clinically plausible for medium-deep brown skin that rarely burns, and it gives users conflicting results. It also treats V and VI as interchangeable when they are distinct categories. Rewrite it so it only applies when the total sits at a band boundary, or add Type IV as a neighboring possibility.
review.notes: The article matches informational intent well. It gives a usable pen-and-paper quiz with a clear table, and it separates Fitzpatrick type from skin tone, undertone and oily/dry skin. It is honest that the scoring is a simplified, unvalidated, non-clinical system. Its handling of deeper skin and its sun-protection and dermatologist referrals are responsible. App claims stay within APP_FACTS: cosmetic skin overview, makeup assistant, virtual makeup try-on, color coordination, Android only with iOS coming soon, and no medical advice. It states plainly that the app cannot determine a Fitzpatrick type. There are no invented stats, testimonials or accuracy claims, and the app section is proportionate rather than promotional. The only blocker is the tie-breaker logic above. Minor points: 'tan' appears as a depth label next to the Q1 'tan' sun-reaction wording, which could confuse readers. Q5 largely duplicates Q2 and Q3, so the quiz double-counts sun reaction. A short note that the Fitzpatrick scale does not measure skin cancer risk would help. The CTA is fine.
